sections.content:
Professor Au adopts a very classical approach in teaching micro theory, he adds quite some stuff to the syllabus, including welfare theorems and general equilibrium, which makes it a very fruitful course.

Personally, the first part of this course is rather boring but I see the need for a UG Econ student to know all these, the second part is game theory which is way more interesting. This course focuses on dynamic games.
sections.teaching: If you’re from his Econ 3113, you’ll already know how amazing he is. Despite teaching this course for the first time, he still maintains top-notch teaching, he prepares for class even when the class is 9 am, also, it’s his first time teaching 2 sessions of the same class, and the crazy thing about his is he can keep the pace at exactly the same page for both classes so I can mess around and go to different classes and not need to be confused. Also, the proofs are easier than those from 3113, so with his explanation, everything is pretty intuitive.
sections.grading:
Mid term: the paper is not so hard (assuming away time constraint), easier than his Econ 3113, but because we’re the first cohort, there’s no past papers, and the questions are pretty different from problem sets so a lot of them require first principle thinking (well that’s the point of an open book exam right), and time is very tight, so I perform worse than 3113 (cuz we all know our TA is Jeremy again who likes to deduct marks from “incomplete” explanation so I need to write a lot of explanation to secure the marks). The questions are deeply conceptual and intuitive, no heavy calculations. (which is pretty insane cuz we’ve been dealing with those terrible calculations the entire time) but ugh this semester there are some questions that benefit people who go to classes cuz the answer is literally spelt out in class (less than 10 marks tho) which some people may find unfair, but anyways.

*Note: I was boring enough to ask AI whether this exam is easier or harder than Econ 3113 and it said this one was harder, so I guess I might be tripping.
*Note: after reading his solution (which is pretty short), I think this exam can be done in 60 minutes, I think I adopted a wrong strategy of trying to explain absolutely everything.

Stat:
sections.workload: Not so much. I think he teaches pretty slowly, and every material is so accessible if you go to class, he is literally feeding you the knowledge, I think the workload is manageable once you’re familiar with his flow (and I have that cuz I took his 3113). The weekly problem sets also make us think hard and are necessary for learning this class as Econ theory aren’t easy in the first place but he simplifies our life A LOT. (Workload is supposed to be horrible if it’s not him teaching, I probably need to spend much more time grasping the concepts)

sections.content: It covers the supply side of the economy, completing the microeconomic theory (ECON 3113 only covers the demand side). The math is normal and straightforward. The ideas are easy to understand. Once you grasp the basic incentive concept, you can handle the entire course.
sections.teaching:
The slides are normal, but they’re clear and easy to read. If you fully understand everything on the slides, you don’t really need to attend the lectures.
I think the tutorial is also unnecessary if you already understand the slides.
sections.grading:
Normal

Just similar to the typical harsh‑grading science or engineering courses (where the mean falls in the C range).

Somehow I think Martin is more willing to give A+.

Be careful with calculations in both the midterm and the final. You can lose a lot of marks from minor arithmetic mistakes.

I thought I’d end up with an A– to A since I wasn’t the highest in either the midterm or the final. But it turned out to be an A+. Thanks, Martin.

1. Intro and Math Review

The content before midterm exam is mostly about optimization using differentiation. The idea is similar to ECON 3113 but in firm side. After midterm, he emphasized a lot on basic game theory.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Martin is humorous in class and chill. He writes down the formula or example on the whiteboard step by step instead of skipping all the derivations, so it will be comfortable.

There is also an improvement in this semester. As Martin said last year's exam involves too many tedious calculation, which resulted in a low average score, he lowered the difficulty level in midterm and taught useful thoughts in midterm review. However, I will say the final is more difficult in midterm in terms of complexity of calculation. At that time I nearly wanted to give up.
sections.grading:
Grading makes sense, mean level is around B-(or B?).
Participation - 5%
Problem Set - 15%
Miderm, final - 35%+45% OR 25%+55%

- A two-sided A4 cheat sheet is allowed in midterm and final. I think it helps a lot.

- The second grading scheme (25+55%) is a special arrangement in this semester. As Prof didn't express clearly to TAs about the time arrangement in midterm, one class was told to have 2 hrs for the exam but they found it wrong when the other class end the exam in 1.5 hrs......Then they had to stop the exam, which might affect students original time allocation. In addition to two grading scheme to choose, he gave grade seperately to the two classroom.

- No idea about how he assessed participation, as Martin didn't raise questions a lot or use IPRS. He just mentions if u only show up on exam, then u will be in trouble.

Midterm - 66/70, lq/mean/uq - 50/55.11/65
Final - 71.5/87, lq/mean/uq - 52.75/59.21/68.5
Overall (assume full mark on hw and participation, based on 35%+45%) - 89.98. Mean - 78.18

Final grade: A
He said a course total above 88% should earn you an A- or better and a score above 76% should earn you a B- or better, with some variation across two classrooms. I think finally he lower the cutoff a bit as I expect an A- based on the statistics.
sections.workload: 8 Problem sets assigned weekly, can work in group (Martin didn't care how large the group is). The mean of each hw is around 23/25 probably because TA's grading is lenient. Not very heavy compared with group project/essay.

sections.content: The course content was well-structured and demonstrated strong coherence, making it easier to follow the theoretical concepts. However, the material felt overly focused on mathematical rigor at times, which could be balanced with more practical examples to illustrate key ideas. Incorporating additional real-world applications or case studies would greatly enhance understanding and make the content more relatable. Overall, the course provides a solid foundation in microeconomic theory, but a greater emphasis on examples would further support and enrich the learning experience.
sections.teaching: While the course included a significant amount of detailed explanations on the mathematical concepts, which at times felt overwhelming, the overall experience was positive. Martin, the instructor, stands out as an exceptionally patient and dedicated teacher. His ability to break down complex ideas and his willingness to support students through challenges truly enhanced the learning experience. Beyond his teaching skills, Martin’s relatable and approachable demeanor—often sharing lighthearted anecdotes about being a responsible dad—added a personal touch that made the course more engaging and enjoyable. Despite the heavy focus on math, Martin’s teaching style and commitment made the material more accessible and the course worthwhile.
sections.grading: I barely studied ...
sections.workload: Alright, one problem sheet per week.

sections.content:
Perhaps it's because I'm from MAEC, I found the content relatively straightforward. The math is quite basic—you should be fine as long as you have a solid understanding of first-order derivatives and Lagrangians.

The math foundations introduced in the first chapter may seem intimidating at first, but they become much more approachable when applied to specific problems in later chapters. So don't worry if you can't understand those immediately in the beginning.
sections.teaching:
I personally enjoyed Martin's teaching style—he’s actually quite funny, and he provides real-life examples in addition to the dry theory.

His math derivations are clearly explained, making them easy to follow. When I had questions after class, he patiently answered each one.
sections.grading:
The grading was fair—nothing out of the ordinary, like any other ECON courses. Some have mentioned that the B range is too narrow, but if you look through older reviews of this course, you’ll see that this grading pattern has been consistent for years. The mean being set at B- isn’t something Martin introduced, so there’s really nothing to complain about on his part.

One positive is that he maximized the A range as much as possible, and he does award A+ grades—unlike some ECON professors who don’t give a single A+ for the entire class.
sections.workload:
The workload for this course is manageable. I got an A+ by doing the following:

1. Attended most of the lectures, understood the derivations, and reviewed all the lecture slides before the exams.
2. Skipped all the tutorials but read most of the notes on my own.
3. Completed all the assignments independently and went through every problem set again on my own before the exam.
4. Attended the last class, as he reviews some important concepts during the session.

sections.content:
Good content about microeconomics. Covers production theory, cost function, profit maximization, game theory, duopoly, and repeated games.

Very interesting intermediate economics theory course. Prepares you well for year 4 econ courses. Requires some basic optimization techniques and a little bit of multivariable calculus to read the lecture proofs. Don’t need too much math to solve the exam, all you need is intuition.
sections.teaching: Martin cares about his students and he tried to make sure everyone understood the materials. He would explain again and again until you get the idea. He is very knowledgeable about economics and delivers the content in interesting ways. There is no lecture recording.
sections.grading:
Very good.
The ta takes off a few marks in homework assignments, but they are inconsequential. Martin tried to give out as many a as possible.

Read and understand the lecture notes before the exam, and you should find most of the questions solvable. The mt is difficult and requires some thinking, but the final is easy enough to work through with almost no math.

sections.content:
Standard micro stuff. Since it was the first semester Martin taught in UST, he followed the textbook tightly:

Textbook: Microeconomic Theory: Basic Principles and Extensions, by Nicholson and Snyder

1. Intro and Math Review (Implicit Function Theorem, Value Function, Envelope Theorem, Kuhn-Tucker Condition, Concave/Convex/Quasi-concave/Quasi-convex)
2. Cost Minimization (Chapters 9 and 10)
3. Profit Maximization (Chapter 11)
4. Partial Equilibrium (Chapter 12)
5. Monopoly (Chapter 13)
6. Externality
7. Game Theory (Chapter 8)
8. Imperfect Competition/Oligopoly (Chapter 15)
9. Repeated Games (Chapter 8)

Basically, this is where you prove your knowledge in ECON2000/3000 level courses in a mathematical way, and then solve tons of optimization problems based on the theories. It gives you the theoretical foundation for ECON4000 level courses. Though universal and sometimes abstract, it's useful.
sections.teaching:
Martin's teaching was OK. His style was like a stand-up comedy, being calm and humorous at the same time. He was also aware of students' reaction to the difficulty of the course content. There were sometimes mistakes in his PowerPoint slights, but he would fix them soon as he found them. The best thing I would say was his prompt reply to questions, no matter online or offline.

But he spent quite some time on trivial math concepts (those we'd learnt from MATH1012/1013 or whatever), assuming students had weak math foundation (on the other hand, there are quite some abstract math tricks required in his exams :( ).

Jeremy was an experienced TA. His tutorials were crucial for you to score high in this course. Don't drop any of those and ask questions. You won't regret following this instruction.
sections.grading:
There were lots of B-rangers out there, because his exams were super hard, and the course was MAEC/ECOF only. But to be objective, he isn't the one to blame, because the university told him to do so. So, f*ck UST.

My scores (Martin adjusted the weight based on people's personal performance, so no idea what happens at last):

Midterm (35%): 46/65
(mean: 39.77, upper: 46, median: 40, lower: 36)
Final (45%): 59/79
(mean: 54.26, upper: 63.13, median: 57, lower: 45.5)

Homework (15%): 25, 25, 24, 23, 25, 25, 23, 24 (full mark: 25 each. Almost full for everyone)
Attendence (5%): No idea

Final grade: B+

I put in quite a lot of effort trying to get across the content, but it turns out that if you are not a math genius, efforts say nothing.

I was in a group of 9. But in fact, only 3 people besides me were actually working (Thank god I had them!). You can see the problem sets were not perfectly done in the "Grading" section.

sections.content:
Please refer to other posts for specific content of this course. Here I just want to write some comment on the course syllabus.
If you have a Chinese cultural background, you'll understand when I say this course is chicken rib. (It refers to something that is a waste to dispose of, but of little value to keep.) I take this course just because it's my major requirement. The course does not focus on the understanding of economic concept. Most of the concepts introduced in this course are very shallow and I think even someone who don't understand a thing about economics can understand them rather quickly. Sometimes I can't help but feel this course should be called applied (high school) maths. Because at the end of the course, I honestly don't know what it is that I learned through this course. So even ECON3113 is this course's prerequisite, you'll feel that this course is a down-grade. (If you have taken Prof. Leung's ECON3113, you'll feel that you did learn something in that course. ) But if you are here just for the grade, this is a course where practice makes perfect and every bit of your effort is likely to pay off. (As opposed to some courses where you simply can't do well no matter how many efforts you make.)
sections.teaching: Teaching is okay. The bad thing is that there's nothing too good about Prof. Huang's teaching, but the good thing is that there's nothing too bad about it either. However, considering this is UST where tons of professors have less than no idea how to teach properly, I'd say he's pretty good. And he speaks good English. That's another thing not every professor in UST can do. He types lecture notes using latex, which are very clear for most parts, so you don't have to take notes yourself. (Now that I think about it, maybe I should give him an A, haha :b)
sections.grading:
I haven't taken final exam yet, so I'll update you on this later.

But I can say something before I know my grade. The key to doing well in exams is to memorise all the formulae and to calculate fast. I have a bit of OCD so I have to check my results over and over again before moving on, which prevents me from doing well in midterm. I won't blame anyone for not having a high score, but a university level exam that only requires good memory and fast calculation to do well? I'd say it's pretty debatable.

Edit: (These words were written after the letter grade came out.)
It's hard to judge whether grading is good without knowing the distribution of the whole class, but bad grading would be a plausible deduction. But before talking about my deduction I just want to say the final exam is much more fair than midterm. On one hand sufficient time was allowed to finish all the questions. On the other hand, there's no weird calculations that could take a ridiculously long time. That is, this time your score only depends on whether you know the stuff, but not on how familiar you are with them or how fast you could calculate. I'd call that an improvement.
Turning to the question of grading, so I scored approximately mean in my midterm and quite a bit higher than mean in final and I got B. So I think it'd be reasonable to say that this is another of UST's "you score mean you get C range" nonsense. Please correct me in comment if I'm wrong. I would welcome the information.
Some additional thoughts (you can skip if you only care about information concerning this course itself): ECON department really needs to reconsider the grading distribution of ECON3113/3123/3133/3143, and maybe even ECON3334. The four theory courses are only taken by ECOF and MAEC students. And there's extra requirement to get into these two majors compared with a regular ECON major. In some sense these courses should be considered ECON dept's "Honour Course Series" and they should offer better grading. But then again, this is UST where they have to make students uncomfortable, so I guess it is what it is. Please forgive my negativity.
sections.workload: A lot of people say this course has a heavy workload. Well, in some sense, it's true. The homework is almost weekly, which can be suffocating at times. But for a 4-credit course, I'd say it's fair. The problem with this course, though, is that it asks us to make inefficient efforts. A lot of questions in the homework are repetitive, and most of them are just about the calculation. Deep understanding of economic concept is almost never tested. So yes, it can be quite frustrating when you spend hours working on a 3000 level economics course, but what you do is merely doing endless, repetitive computation. Personally, I don't feel satisfied because as a university student, I don't feel like doing high school work.

sections.content:
This course continues from 3113, where 3113 derive demand function from individual consumer utility maximization problem, the first half this course will talk about firms and construct supply curves.

1. Firm Production Function
How does the firm cost to produce a target amount of quantity of goods. Introduction to different production function and function types/jargons.

2. Firm Cost Minimization on given quantity supplied
How should the firm choose between different inputs to produce a target amount of supply. Derive Cost as a function of quantity supplied.

3. Firm Profit Maximization Problem
Facing different market structure, how should the firm choose how much to supply in order to maximize profit. Introducing shut-down point and LR exit point. Extension of content in ECON2103/2113.

4. Partial Equilibrium Competitive Model
Comparative statics: How can we predict the changes of market outcome given particular changes. Very useful but a lot of formula included.
Welfare analysis: price ceiling, tax, international trade, DWL...

5. Monopoly
Monopoly market equilibrium; Price discrimination

---Part 1 finishes---
6. Game Theory
Introduction of static game, sequential game, repeated game, tacit collusion.

7. Oligopoly
The best topic in this course, Bertrand Model; Cournot Model; Stackelberg Model; Hotelling Model; Firm entry deterrence.

8. Public Good and Externality
How the overall welfare of a society can be improved?

This course is designed in a bit mechanical way, meaning that you can still do a bunch of calculations and obtain the result with standard procedure, there is no genius tricks that you can do to solve the problems.
This lead to a question that is the understanding of the course material, very often you will be overwhelmed by the math in this course and ignore the rationale/intuition behind the problem. I personally didn't know why I have to set up the equation/optimization problem like that when learning in ch2. It was until ch4 that I know it was intended to obtain a cost function with quantity as input, because we want to derive the market equilibrium which is jointly determined by demand and supply.

After this course you will learn a bunch of useful skills, like comparative statics, how to build up a model/write down the optimization problem. The greatest take away from this course will be the way to build up a model/solve individual agent's problem.

Personally I like the second half of this course as it is more fun using game theory perspective to analyse problems.

sections.grading:
Since this semester is in online mode, the grading scheme is a little bit different.
20% hw
20% attendance
25% midterm
35% final
I think everyone got almost full marks in hw and Sunny said as long as we showed up in the zoom, we would get the attendance points. So I guess everyone got at least 40%.

Understanding concepts helps for exams but what really matters is computational skill. If you are good at computation, you definitely won't get a bad grade. But if you are not confidence in fast computation, I suggest you to at least be really familiar with hw questions which can help you to get used to those math models (basically just differentiation). Also, since we took online exam, Sunny intentionally set exams extremely long. For example, he said there are only four questions in the midterm, but every question had at least 5 sub questions. I think I calculated every question really fast in the final exam, but I still can't finish the last sub-question.

sections.content:
ECON3133 is basically ECON3113 reversed in the sense that you are now dealing with profit maximization rather than utility maximization, with the introduction of Game Theory to analyze oligopoly/market competition. In hindsight, the content is very much similar to what is going on in the later parts of ECON2103/2113.  

Provided that you have a good foundation from Micro Theory I, up until Game Theory should be a breeze.

The D given does not represent what the course is meant to teach, but rather what the professor has decided to put into the course, much of the content is simplified, reduced down compared to the other lectures. To learn the contents, I would suggest going to Prof. Huang's class or go read Snyder's book.
sections.teaching: The prof. English is definitely much clearer compared to other mainland professors in HKUST, however, attending the lectures is not necessary for you to perform well in this course, given that most of what he does in class is simply repeating what is in the slides, albeit much slower.
sections.grading:
The means and statistics could be referenced in Doug's review.

For your reference:
Midterm: 98/100, Final: 52/100
Assignments: Full
Final Grade: B-

What bothers me the most is not how hard the paper was, but rather how the mark was given and how it was handled.

Going back to my point earlier, if the contents were not as trimmed as it is, then perhaps the paper could have been more indicative of what we have actually learnt in class.

Given that the final was open-book (note that being open book or not had practically no difference, as there was no need to memorize anything), and how the solutions tend to be very "minimalistic", this creates a lot of ambiguity in the marking, reflected in how one may not attain full credits in a question, even though his/her answers are nearly an exact match to the suggested solutions.
sections.workload:
The workload is pretty much non-existent for this course, given that you could cram it all before the night of the midterm/final and still perform to a decent level.

The assignments are also judged based on completeness, which implies that you only need to write something down, just to indicate that you "attempted" the questions.

Note: If you want to really learn the content, then the workload incurred by either sitting the other prof. class or reading Snyder's book, online materials may downgrade it from A to C.

sections.grading:
I want to particularly emphasize on grading
As other mentions, this course is hard, competitive, and the distribution is so narrow. It is just easy to fall into C range

I personally have an overall score below mean 1% and get a C+, meanwhile, my friend above mean 1% get a B. The cutoff is just crazily close.

So, please be reminded that it is not a good grade course for average people. The traditional UST grading "mean = B-/C+" still valid here, even though I agree with others' review mentioned that this course provides excellent content and sunny is indeed a nice and perfect professor, but, for the grading part, I feel I really need to tell you guys, IT IS NOT GREAT!

sections.content:
第二個intermediate micro course。同3113比，個course個廣度係廣好多好多，但深度又好似無3113咁深，好多野都只係略略帶過，無咁多proofs。基本上係ECON2113嘅加深同重數版，頭1/4個course講firm theory，之後就擺埋demand同supply一齊，討論唔同嘅competition market同埋用game theory去推一啲market outcome。最後就補返3113無教嘅externalities同public goods。數學上嚟講會重數過3113，但唔使理解得好似3113咁透徹，好多時都係好公式化咁計。主要嚟講都係用first order condition同Lagrangian 去計數，solve equations set嘅時候小心啲就得。同埋最緊要知自己有啲咩variables郁得有咩唔郁得。其實最後呢個course最重要唔係學左幾多個唔同嘅models，而係學個思維方法(methodology)。

Course Content:
1. Math review

2. Firm Theory: （淨係呢part已經等於3113大半個sem)
  2.1. Production function
  2.2. Cost minimization problem (基本上同3113個utility maximization大同小異）
  2.3. Properties of cost function
  2.4. Profit maximization problem of a price taking firm
  2.5. Profit maximization problem of a monopoly and its relation with elasticity of demand

3. Partial Equilibrium:
  3.1. Demand and supply
  3.2. Short run and long run equilibrium
  3.3. Comparative statics (全個course最重數嘅位，講緊點用elasticity去estimate啲changes，亦都好有用。）
  3.4. Welfare analysis
-------------------midterm---------------------
4. Monopoly:
  4.1. Monopolistic competition
  4.2. Monopoly behavior
  4.3. Regulating monopoly
  4.4. Price discrimination

5. Game Theory:
  5.1. Simultaneous move game
  5.2. Pure strategy Nash equilibrium and mixed strategy Nash equilibrium
  5.3. Sequential move game
  5.4. Subgame Perfect equilibrium (無考到）
  5.5. Repeated game

6. Imperfect Competition: (主要係講duopoly/oligopoly)
  6.1. Bertrand price competition model
  6.2. Cournot quantity competition model
  6.3. Bertrand differentiated product competition model
  6.4. Hotelling model（要solve嘅話要solve成個鐘）
  6.5. Stackelberg leader-follower model
  6.6. Merger and collusion

7. Externalities and Public Goods: (會用返3113啲utility maximization)
  7.1. Externalities
  7.2. Public goods
sections.teaching:
Sunny教書好鬼正，個人都幾搞笑。但佢會講得幾急幾快下。佢個power point slide 會有唔同concept，之後會有啲example，sunny就會用visualizer 喺紙到由頭教我地solve一次，幾有耐心。佢啲英文極好聽，唔會一舊舊，而且佢識廣東話，問問題可以用廣東話問，溝通完全無問題。今個sem因為時代革命，11月後期要用zoom上堂。成件事好反智，不過sunny用zoom會share screen即時打latex，同佢用紙筆solve一樣，完全唔會有問題，佢仲要打得好快。每個chapter完咗佢都會有啲discussion，可能係一啲real life application/issues，但其實好多時同佢個chapter教嘅野唔係咁related同埋大家都知佢唔考都唔係好聽，但其實佢講嘅野好多都好有意思，例如佢有一次講點解程序公義咁重要。喺咁嘅時勢，大家作為大學生都唔應該淨喺掛住個grade，唔同嘅知識都要多啲吸收同了解。

tutor係shi xiang，基本上係冇鬼用，啲tutorial notes離地到傻，佢啲字又核突睇唔明，講野又講到一舊舊，assignment又突登少少野都捉，唔會俾full你，有仲差過無。
sections.grading:
一個midterm一個final，七份assignment（suppose係八份但今個semester cut咗一份）。考試基本上主要考計數，無咩點考concept/ application。Final係cumulative，但考落其實無咩點考midterm前嘅野。Grade嚟講我覺得佢應該係A range好闊，但如果你aim A+就應該唔太易，原因一嚟啲人太勁，二嚟就係sunny都應該大部分會派A，就唔會係A+同A-。

Grading scheme:
Assignment 10%
Midterm 30%
Final 60%

General Performance:
Assignment: I guess most of the people get nearly full in this part
Midterm: 63.4/100
Final: 92.3/110

My Performance:

Final Grade: A

你話好唔好grade呢，我會話差過3113囉，同埋啲同學真係好勁，想考A+基本上要95%先有機會。
sections.workload: 如果你認真對待呢個course，係算重workload。佢基本上每個星期一份assignment，但係佢每份assignment都長到七彩，每次都交十幾廿版A4紙，不停喺到計計計。每個星期都要俾幾個鐘佢係到鋤。另外因為個course太廣太多material，溫exam都會溫得幾痛苦下。不過啲assignment認真做真係對考試好有幫助。
